description: Ireland, Scotland, the Dutch War — and the army turning on its own Parliament.
content_html:
The Rump Parliament and Its Problems

The Rump Parliament that governed England after 1649 was a small, self-selected body with limited popular legitimacy. It faced immediate and urgent threats: Royalist Ireland and a Scotland that had proclaimed Charles II king. Its relationship with Oliver Cromwell — and with the army that had created it — was tense from the start. Parliament wanted to control the army; the army believed it had a godly mission that Parliament was obstructing.

Cromwell in Ireland 1649

In August 1649 Cromwell led an army to Ireland to suppress the Catholic Confederation and Royalist alliance. His campaign included two sieges that became a permanent part of Irish historical memory. At Drogheda in September 1649, approximately 3,500 people were killed after the garrison refused surrender. Cromwell justified this under the contemporary laws of war: a garrison that refused terms and was then stormed forfeited its right to quarter. At Wexford the following month, a similar number were killed, including many civilians, when soldiers acted before Cromwell had given orders.

Historians debate how to assess these events. Cromwell himself wrote that the deaths at Drogheda were “a righteous judgement of God upon these barbarous wretches”, citing the 1641 Irish Rebellion as justification. Critics argue the civilian deaths at Wexford in particular went beyond even the brutal norms of seventeenth-century warfare. The Cromwellian conquest of Ireland also involved mass transplantation of Catholic landowners and significant land confiscation. These events remained deeply embedded in Irish collective memory for centuries.

Key Fact

At Drogheda (September 1649) approximately 3,500 were killed; at Wexford (October 1649) a similar number died including civilians. Cromwell justified Drogheda under laws of war covering sieges where surrender was refused.

Scotland: Dunbar and Worcester

Charles II had been proclaimed king by the Scots, who accepted him after he agreed to the Covenant. Cromwell moved against Scotland in 1650. At the Battle of Dunbar (3 September 1650) Cromwell won against superior numbers after the Scots were manoeuvred into an unfavourable position by their Presbyterian ministers, who insisted on purging “ungodly” officers before the battle. Charles then led a Scottish army south into England, hoping for English Royalist support that largely failed to materialise. At the Battle of Worcester (3 September 1651) — exactly one year after Dunbar — Cromwell crushed this force. Charles escaped in famous circumstances (hiding in an oak tree at Boscobel) and eventually reached France after six weeks on the run.

The Rump also pursued an aggressive commercial and foreign policy. The Navigation Act of 1651 required goods imported to England to be carried in English ships or ships of the producing country, directly targeting Dutch carrying trade. The First Anglo-Dutch War (1652–1654) followed. The Rump thus demonstrated an assertive Protestant republic could pursue national commercial interests — but the cost and inconclusive nature of the war added to its unpopularity.

Cromwell Dissolves the Rump: April 1653

By 1652–53 Cromwell had grown increasingly frustrated with the Rump. It had sat for thirteen years, showed little inclination to hold elections that might replace it, and was resisting army pressure for godly reformation of the law and church. On 20 April 1653, Cromwell entered the House of Commons with armed soldiers, berated MPs in famously contemptuous terms (“you are no Parliament”), and physically ejected them. The Speaker was removed from his chair. This act destroyed the constitutional continuity of the English republic — henceforth governance rested openly on military power.

Key Fact

Cromwell dissolved the Rump in April 1653 because it refused to dissolve itself and hold elections, blocked godly legal reform, and acted in what he saw as narrow self-interest. The dissolution showed the army, not Parliament, held real power.

Cromwell believed he was acting on God’s behalf. His victories at Dunbar and Worcester had confirmed divine favour. But critics noted the contradiction: Parliament had fought to defend constitutional government, and now the army had made itself the ultimate authority. George Monck and other army figures tolerated this in the short term. The Rump’s dissolution left England without any constitutional settlement — exactly the problem Cromwell spent the rest of his rule trying to solve.
exam_tip_html: When answering questions about Cromwell’s role in this period, keep his actions in Ireland and his dissolution of the Rump as analytically separate issues — they happened for different reasons. The Irish campaign was military necessity; the Rump’s dissolution was political frustration. Examiners expect candidates to explain Cromwell’s reasons, not just describe what he did. The Drogheda and Wexford evidence is well-documented — use specific figures rather than vague references to ‘many deaths’.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Cromwell’s Irish campaign (1649) included the storming of Drogheda (c.3,500 killed) and Wexford; the Scottish campaigns ended at Worcester (September 1651) with Charles II’s escape.
  • The Navigation Act (1651) targeted Dutch trade, leading to the First Anglo-Dutch War (1652–54).
  • Cromwell dissolved the Rump Parliament in April 1653, basing power openly on military force and leaving England without a constitutional settlement.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Cromwell's campaign in Ireland in 1649.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: One accurate feature with supporting detail. Example: At the siege of Drogheda in September 1649, Cromwell's forces stormed the garrison after it refused surrender, killing approximately 3,500 people including soldiers and civilians.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Navigation Act of 1651.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Feature 1: The Navigation Act required goods imported to England to be carried in English ships or ships of the producing country. Feature 2: It was designed to damage Dutch carrying trade and promote English commercial interests, leading directly to the First Anglo-Dutch War (1652-54).

practice_questions.text: Explain why Cromwell dissolved the Rump Parliament in April 1653.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple reasons (Rump refused to hold elections, blocked godly reform, sat too long, narrow self-interest) linked with analysis of the deeper tension between army mission and parliamentary authority. Secure: Two reasons with evidence. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Cromwell's military campaigns in Ireland (1649) were justified. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument considering Cromwell's own justification (laws of war, 1641 rebellion), evidence from Drogheda and Wexford (documented death tolls), contemporary norms of siege warfare, and the specific circumstances at Wexford where soldiers acted without orders. Reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Considers both sides with evidence. Developing: One-sided. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Cromwell won the Battle of Dunbar in September 1650.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains Cromwell's military skill, Scottish Presbyterian ministers' decision to purge 'ungodly' officers before the battle, Scottish army manoeuvred into unfavourable terrain, numerical disadvantage overcome by discipline. Secure: Two reasons with evidence. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the relationship between the Rump Parliament and Cromwell became increasingly difficult 1649–1653.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains different views of the republic's purpose (Parliament's narrow interest vs army's godly mission), Rump's refusal to dissolve, blocking of legal reform, army's frustration after military victories, leading to dissolution. Secure: Two reasons. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple.

glossary_terms.definition: The remnant of the Long Parliament left after Pride's Purge; it governed England as a republic 1649-1653 until Cromwell dissolved it.
Son of Charles I, proclaimed King by the Scots in 1649, defeated at Worcester in 1651, restored to the English throne in 1660.
Parliamentary and Puritan military leader, dominant figure in English politics 1649-1658, became Lord Protector in December 1653.
Town in County Louth where Cromwell's forces stormed the garrison in September 1649; around 3,500 people were killed, including soldiers and civilians.
Town on the south-east coast of Ireland stormed by Cromwell's forces in October 1649, with significant civilian casualties.
Battle fought on 3 September 1650 where Cromwell's army defeated the Scottish Covenanting army, opening the road to Edinburgh.
The final battle of the Civil War period, fought at Worcester on 3 September 1651, where Cromwell destroyed Charles II's army; Charles escaped and eventually reached France.
Parliamentary legislation of 1651 requiring goods imported to England to be carried in English ships or ships of the country of origin, damaging Dutch trade.

hero_image_caption: Cromwell consolidated the republic through military campaigns in Ireland, Scotland and at sea.
